items.text: COMMITTEE DISCHARGED AND COMMITTED TO RULES

items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the penal law, in relation to prohibiting sex offenders from playing augmented reality games
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S2652

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the penal law, in relation to prohibiting sex
offenders from playing augmented reality games

 PURPOSE :

This bill will create a new class of digital games in the penal law,
and will prevent sex offenders under supervision pursuant to penal law
65.10 from playing such games.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1: Adds accessing an augmented reality game to the activities
which sex offenders are prohibiting from engaging in when under a
sentence of probation or conditional discharge. Defines augmented
reality games.

Section 2: The act shall take effect 60 days after it becomes law.

 EXISTING LAW :

Under current law, augmented reality games are not defined, and sex
offenders are not explicitly prohibited from accessing them while on
probation or conditional discharge.

 JUSTIFICATION :

Augmented reality games are a new class of games that allow users to
engage in scenarios that combine elements of the real world with
fictional elements which are part of the game. These games are often
played on smartphones and tablets, as they usually require the user to
move around from place to place to satisfy certain in-game objectives.

Some of these games, such as the massively popular "Pokemon GO" are
like modern scavenger hunts. They send a user outside his/her home to
real-world locations in order to find rare characters/items to gain
more power within the game. Pokemon GO is the first massively popular
augmented reality game, and within less than a month of its
publishing, has garnered 30 million downloads between the iOS and
Google Play app stores.

However, because both children and adults are encouraged to play these
games, (Pokemon GO lists its target audience as all those over ten
years of age), there are inherent risks for unsupervised children.
The IDC has conducted an investigation that has revealed valuable
in-game objectives on the property of sex offenders' residences. It
also discovered at least one instance where a known sex offender was
playing the game with a child in public.

Certain sex offenders, while on probation or conditional discharge,
are prohibited from engaging in certain high-risk activities that
could endanger youth or encourage the sex offender's illegal behavior.
These activities include accessing social networking websites,
accessing pornographic material, etc. The usage of augmented reality
games, as they become more popular, could expose these dangerous sex
offenders to children as both the children and sex offenders are
encouraged to congregate at the same locations in the game and
interact in the real-world while playing the game. If a sex offender
is prevented from accessing a social networking website, where they do
not have direct physical access to children, they should certainly be
prevented from playing these augmented reality games, where they
inevitably will come in close proximity to children.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

2016 - S. 8174 - In Senate Rules

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None.

 LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect on the sixtieth day after it shall have
become a law.

BILL NUMBER:  S2652A

 TITLE OF BILL :  An act to amend the executive law and the penal law,
in relation to prohibiting sex offenders from playing augmented
reality games

 PURPOSE :

This bill will prohibit level 2 and level 3 sex offenders on probation
or parole from accessing augmented reality games

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1: Prohibits level 2 and 3 sex offenders on parole from
accessing augmented reality games. Defines augmented reality games.

Section 2: Prohibits level 2 and 3 sex offenders on probation or
conditional discharge from accessing augmented reality games. Defines
augmented reality games.

Section 3: The act shall take effect 60 days after it becomes law.
